title: GameSpot Veteran Lucy James Quits to Launch Game Discovery Newsletter with Geoff Keighley’s Player.gg
summary:
Imagine opening your inbox to find a secret code that lets you play an unreleased PC game before anyone else. That’s the promise of lookingfor.game, a brand-new weekly newsletter from Lucy James, who just left GameSpot after 12 years. James, who is co-hosting Summer Game Fest Live with Geoff Keighley, told Kotaku that while GameSpot was “an extremely special place,” she’s been itching to dive into the indie game scene. “I’ve known for a while that I wanted to pursue something in the indie game space,” she said, “and when everything aligned with Geoff and FirstLook, I knew I just had to make the jump.”

FirstLook is a “player relationship platform” that helps developers run private playtests — it’s already used by publishers like Krafton (Subnautica 2) and Remedy Entertainment (Alan Wake 2). Now, FirstLook is launching Player.gg, a discovery layer that will track new game announcements, recommend titles, and organize your Steam wishlists. James’s newsletter will be hosted on Player.gg, giving it direct integration with Steam and the Internet Game Database (IGDB) to pull in game info automatically. “FirstLook understands gamers,” James said, contrasting it with mainstream newsletter platforms like Substack or beehiiv, which she felt lacked the gaming-specific tech and attention the project needed.

Player.gg also allows curators like James to partner with studios for exclusive beta invites or paid promotions, creating a potential virtuous cycle that benefits both players and developers. Summer Game Fest will serve as the first major test of the platform’s usefulness. While James’s newsletter remains wholly owned by her, the partnership with Keighley and FirstLook signals a serious attempt to solve the perennial problem of game discovery in an increasingly crowded market. As James put it, “I’m excited to build a community and start sharing awesome games.”
why_it_matters: This story shows how the way people find new games is shifting from traditional reviews to direct‑to‑player communities, and how a single creator can now build an influential platform with the right tech partners — potentially changing which games become hits.

background_read: Lucy James is a well-known video game journalist and presenter who spent 12 years at GameSpot, one of the world's most popular gaming websites.
Geoff Keighley, a Canadian video game journalist, is famous for creating The Game Awards and Summer Game Fest — two major events where publishers announce new games and hardware.

FirstLook is a platform designed to help game studios manage feedback from selected players before a game's release. Publishers like Krafton (the South Korean company behind PUBG) and Remedy Entertainment (the Finnish studio that made Alan Wake) already use it for private playtests.

In the past, newsletters about games often relied on separate email tools like Substack, but those didn't have built-in connections to gaming ecosystems like the Internet Game Database (IGDB) or Steam, which tracks wishlists and recommendations.

The 'virtuous cycle' mentioned in the article refers to a model where influential curators give players access to exclusive betas, which makes the newsletter more popular, which then attracts more developers, creating a self-reinforcing loop of discovery.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Imagine opening your inbox to find a secret code that lets you play an unreleased PC game before anyone else.
KEY EVENT: Veteran GameSpot host Lucy James quits after 12 years to launch a game‑discovery newsletter on a new platform.
├─ WHO: Lucy James, co‑hosting Summer Game Fest; Geoff Keighley and FirstLook as partners.
├─ WHAT: A newsletter called 'lookingfor.game' that integrates directly with Steam and IGDB.
└─ DETAIL: The newsletter is owned by James, not the platform, and will be hosted on Player.gg.
TECH & REASON: James chose Player.gg over Substack/beehiiv because it understands gamers and connects to game databases automatically.
PLATFORM POWER: FirstLook already helps publishers (Krafton, Remedy) run private playtests; Player.gg adds discovery features.
BENEFITS: Curators can partner with studios for exclusive beta invites or paid promotions, aiming to create a virtuous cycle.
OPEN TEST: Summer Game Fest will be the first real‑world trial of Player.gg's usefulness.

perspectives.description: Players gain early access to secret betas and a trusted source to cut through the noise of thousands of releases. Indie developers, often ignored by big media, can reach a dedicated audience through a curated newsletter, giving them a fairer shot at success.

Paid promotions could blur the line between genuine enthusiasm and advertising, making it hard for readers to know if a 'recommendation' is truly independent. The platform's heavy integration with Steam and a single curator may also concentrate power in too few hands, silencing smaller voices.

The industry has long struggled with discoverability — the more games are released, the harder it is for any single title to be noticed. James's partnership mirrors a broader trend of 'human curation' returning as an answer to algorithm fatigue, similar to what music and film services have attempted.

If the Player.gg model succeeds, we might see a wave of game‑first newsletter platforms, forcing legacy media to adapt or decline. The real test will be whether such systems can remain trustworthy once money and exclusive access are deeply intertwined.
